insight: The map shows how ready each province is for small hydropower projects. Scores range from 2.29 to 35.46 on a 0‑100 scale, with most provinces falling into the very low or low groups. Even places with lots of rivers or wet land can score low because hydropower needs two things: enough water flow and a good hydraulic head, which is the height drop that water can fall. A higher drop means more energy, like water rushing down a steep hill versus a gentle slope. Provinces such as Pampanga (score 2.29, hydraulic head only 11 m), Tarlac (3.19, head 15.7 m) and Bulacan (3.47, head 17 m) have flat terrain, so the water does not fall far enough to generate much power. In contrast, Nueva Vizcaya (35.46, head 196.7 m), Catanduanes (33.25, head 167.6 m) and Romblon (31.69, head 153.8 m) have steeper gradients, giving them the highest scores in this view, though they are still classified as low because other factors like overall water volume are modest. The pattern shows that simply having water is not enough; the landscape’s slope and height drop are crucial for turning water into useful electricity.
